nameStory: The name "Adam's needle" comes from the plant's sharp, sword-like leaves that are pointed enough to use as a sewing needle. The "thread" part refers to the curly white fibers that peel away from the leaf edges, providing nature's own sewing thread to go with the needle!
description: Common yucca is a striking evergreen shrub that looks like it belongs in a desert but has adapted to life in New England gardens. It forms a dense rosette of sword-shaped, blue-green leaves that stay green year-round, creating a dramatic architectural focal point. The plant typically grows 2-3 feet tall and wide, but can send up spectacular flower spikes reaching up to 10 feet tall when it blooms.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, sword-shaped leaves arranged in a tight rosette, blue-green in color with sharp points that can actually puncture skin. The leaf edges have distinctive white, curly fibers that peel away naturally, giving them a slightly fuzzy appearance.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Creamy white, bell-shaped flowers hang downward in drooping clusters along a tall central spike. Each flower is about 2 inches long and feels waxy to the touch, blooming in late spring to early summer.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a symmetrical, spiky rosette that stays low to the ground, looking almost like a giant green sea urchin. Multiple rosettes often cluster together over time as the plant spreads.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops large, oval seed pods that split open when ripe to reveal flat, black seeds. The pods are about 2 inches long and feel papery when mature.

habitat: In New England, common yucca is almost exclusively found in cultivated settings like gardens, parks, and landscaped areas, as it's not native to the region. It thrives in well-drained, sandy soils and full sun locations, often planted as an ornamental for its drought tolerance and architectural form.

seasonality.spring: New growth appears as bright green shoots in the center of the rosette, and the dramatic flower spike begins to emerge in late spring.
seasonality.summer: The spectacular white flower display peaks in early summer, creating a towering spike of drooping, bell-shaped blooms that attract night-flying moths.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods ripen and split open, while the evergreen leaves remain unchanged, maintaining their blue-green color and spiky appearance.
seasonality.winter: The rosette stays completely evergreen, providing year-round structure in the landscape, though the leaves may take on slightly more blue or purple tints in cold weather.

funFact: Yucca flowers can only be pollinated by a single species of tiny white moth in a partnership so specific that neither can survive without the other - the female moth deliberately collects pollen to feed her larvae, making her one of the only insects that actively pollinates rather than doing it accidentally!
confusionNotes: In New England gardens, it's sometimes confused with ornamental grasses or other spiky plants like daylilies, but the thick, rigid, sharp-pointed leaves with curly white fibers are unmistakable. Remember: if it looks dangerous to touch and has fuzzy leaf edges, it's likely yucca!
contextualKnowledge: Despite its desert appearance, this southeastern US native has proven surprisingly cold-hardy in New England gardens. Many people assume all yuccas are tropical, but this species can handle New England winters when planted in well-drained soil.
compareHints: Common yucca has the most prominent curly white fibers along its leaf edges compared to its relatives. Weak-leaf yucca has softer, more flexible leaves that bend rather than staying rigidly upright, while moundlily yucca has broader leaves and grows much taller overall, sometimes reaching tree-like proportions.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Weak-leaf yucca is distinguished from common yucca by its notably flexible leaves that bend rather than remaining rigid, and from moundlily yucca by its ground-hugging rosette growth habit rather than forming a trunk.
Moundlily yucca has broader, blue-green leaves with relatively soft tips compared to common yucca's narrow, dark green leaves with sharp points and curly white threads.
